clips.send: Dont mix up: Bubble sort is very fast on a list that is already nearly sorted — one pass with no swaps and it stops.
clips.text: Dont mix up: Bubble sort is very fast on a list that is already nearly sorted — one pass with no swaps and it stops.

clips.send: Bubble sort. Walk along the list comparing neighbours; swap them if they are in the wrong order. Big values “bubble” to the end. Compare items 1 and 2, swap if needed; then 2 and 3; … to the end. After one pass the biggest item is in its place. Repeat passes until a pass makes no swaps. Worst case for n items: n(n minus 1)/2 comparisons — 10 items equals 45, 1,000 items about 500,000.

clips.send: Dont mix up: Insertion sort and selection sort are both O(n squared ), but insertion sort gets much faster when the data is nearly sorted; selection sort never does.
clips.text: Dont mix up: Insertion sort and selection sort are both O(n²), but insertion sort gets much faster when the data is nearly sorted; selection sort never does.

clips.send: Binary search. In a sorted list, look at the middle item. Too big? Throw away the right half. Too small? Throw away the left half. Repeat. Each guess halves what is left: 100, 50, 25, 13, 7, 4, 2, 1. At most 7 guesses for 100, 10 for 1,000, 20 for 1,000,000. Doubling the list adds only ONE more guess.

clips.send: Dont mix up: Linear search is not “wrong” — for a short or unsorted list it is the best you can do.

clips.send: Breadth-first search. Explore a maze like a spreading wave: first every square 1 step away, then 2 steps, then 3… The first time the wave reaches the exit, that is the shortest path. Needs a map of the whole maze (the robot’s rules don’t). GPS route planners use relatives of this idea (like Dijkstra’s algorithm).

clips.send: Merge sort. Split the list into tiny pieces, then merge pieces back together in order — two sorted piles merge quickly. A list of 1 item is already sorted. Merge pairs of 1 into sorted 2s, then 2s into 4s, 4s into 8s…. To merge, compare the fronts of two piles and take the smaller. About n·log2n comparisons: 1,000 items about 10,000 instead of 500,000.
clips.text: Merge sort. Split the list into tiny pieces, then merge pieces back together in order — two sorted piles merge quickly.. A list of 1 item is already sorted.. Merge pairs of 1 into sorted 2s, then 2s into 4s, 4s into 8s…. To merge, compare the fronts of two piles and take the smaller.. About n·log₂n comparisons: 1,000 items ≈ 10,000 instead of 500,000.

clips.send: Quick sort. Pick a “pivot” (here: the last item). Move everything smaller to its left, everything bigger to its right. Then quick-sort each side. One pass around the pivot puts the pivot in its final place. Each side is a smaller problem: divide and conquer, like merge sort, but in place. Average: about 1.4·n·log2n comparisons — O(n log n). Bad luck: if the pivot is always the biggest or smallest (try Already sorted!), it needs n(n minus 1)/2 — O(n squared ).

clips.send: Linear search. Check items one by one from the start until you find what you want. Works on any list, sorted or not. Worst case: n looks (the item is last or missing). Ctrl+F in a document is a kind of linear search.

clips.send: Selection sort. Find the smallest item and put it first; then find the smallest of the rest and put it second; and so on. Scan the whole unsorted part to find the smallest. Swap it to the front of the unsorted part. The sorted part grows by one each round. Always about n(n minus 1)/2 comparisons, even if the list was already sorted.

clips.send: Insertion sort. Like sorting playing cards in your hand: take the next card and slide it left until it sits in the right place. The left part is always sorted; it starts with 1 item. Take the next item and compare it with its left neighbour; swap while the neighbour is bigger. Already sorted list: only n minus 1 comparisons and 0 moves — the best case. Reversed list: n(n minus 1)/2 comparisons — the worst case, O(n squared ).

clips.send: What is an algorithm? An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step method that always finishes and solves a problem. A recipe is an algorithm for a cake. Same input, same steps, same answer, every time. Computer scientists compare algorithms by counting steps, not by timing one computer. Click a lane (bubble, selection or merge) to see its steps.

clips.send: 插入排序。就像整理手里的扑克牌：拿起下一张，把它往左挪，直到放进正确的位置。左边部分始终是排好的，一开始只有1个数。拿出下一个数，和左边的邻居比较；邻居更大就交换，一直往左挪。已经排好的列表：只要n减1次比较、0次移动——最好情况。完全倒序的列表：n(n减1)/2次比较——最坏情况，O(n 的平方 )。

clips.send: 快速排序。选一个“基准”（这里选最后一个数）。比它小的都放到左边，比它大的都放到右边。再分别对两边做快速排序。围绕基准分一次，基准就到了它最终的位置。两边各是一个更小的问题：和归并排序一样分而治之，但不需要额外空间。平均：大约1.4·n·log2n次比较——O(n log n)。运气不好：如果基准总是最大或最小的（试试“已排好”！），就要n(n减1)/2次——O(n 的平方 )。

clips.send: 归并排序。把列表拆成很小的块，再把块按顺序合并回去——两堆已经排好的数合并起来很快。只有1个数的列表本来就是有序的。把1个1个合并成有序的2个，再把2个合并成4个，4个合并成8个……。合并时，比较两堆最前面的数，取小的那个。大约n·log2n次比较：1000个数约1万次，而不是50万次。

clips.send: 二分查找。在排好序的列表里看正中间那个。太大？扔掉右半边；太小？扔掉左半边。重复。每猜一次剩下的减半：100，50，25，13，7，4，2，1。100个数最多猜7次，1000个最多10次，100万个最多20次。列表变成两倍长，只需要多猜一次。

clips.send: 广度优先搜索。像水波一样探索迷宫：先找所有1步能到的格子，再找2步、3步……水波第一次碰到出口时，走过的就是最短路线。它需要整个迷宫的地图（机器人的规则不需要）。导航软件规划路线用的就是它的“亲戚”（例如迪杰斯特拉算法）。

clips.send: 冒泡排序。沿着列表比较相邻的两个数，顺序不对就交换。大的数像气泡一样“冒”到最后。比较第1和第2个，需要就交换；再比较第2和第3个……一直到最后。走完一趟，最大的数就到了它的位置。一趟一趟重复，直到某一趟一次交换都没有。n个数的最坏情况：n(n减1)/2次比较——10个数要45次，1000个数约50万次。

clips.send: 什么是算法？算法是一套准确的、一步一步的方法，它一定会结束，并且能解决问题。菜谱就是做蛋糕的算法。同样的输入，同样的步骤，同样的结果，每次都一样。计算机科学家比较算法时数“步数”，而不是看某台电脑跑了几秒。点击一条跑道（冒泡、选择或归并），看它的步骤。

clips.send: 选择排序。找出最小的放到第一个；再从剩下的里找最小的放到第二个；依此类推。扫描整个未排序部分，找出最小的。把它换到未排序部分的最前面。每一轮，已排好的部分多一个。总是大约n(n减1)/2次比较，即使列表本来就排好了。
